title: World Facts — 10 True/False
description: A richer LC-JSON question-set example: 10 standalone trueFalseQuestion entries spanning geography, science, history, and common misconceptions. Each question carries hint text, per-question feedback, and topic tags. Use this as a template for hand-authored TF banks targeting the QuestionSet artifact.

questions.title: Earth's Natural Satellites
questions.hint: Earth has only one body that orbits it naturally. Other planets like Mars (Phobos, Deimos) or Jupiter have many.
questions.prompt: The Earth has only one natural satellite.

feedback.correct: Correct — the Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. (Several thousand artificial satellites also orbit Earth, but those don't count as 'natural'.)
feedback.incorrect: Actually true. The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. You may be thinking of artificial satellites — there are thousands of those — but Earth has just one natural moon.

questions.title: Tallest Mountain on Earth
questions.hint: Be careful with the wording: 'tallest base-to-peak' is not the same as 'highest above sea level'.
questions.prompt: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from base to peak.

feedback.correct: Correct — Everest has the highest peak above sea level (8,849 m), but Mauna Kea in Hawaii is the tallest from base to peak: about 10,200 m, with most of it underwater.
feedback.incorrect: Actually false. Everest is the highest peak above sea level, but Mauna Kea (Hawaii) is taller measured base-to-peak — around 10,200 m, with most of it submerged.

questions.title: Australia: Country and Continent
questions.prompt: Australia is both a country and a continent.

feedback.correct: Correct — Australia is unique in this regard. The country occupies the entire continental landmass.
feedback.incorrect: Actually true. Australia is one of the seven continents and the country covers the whole continental landmass.

questions.title: First People in the Americas
questions.hint: Distinguish 'first humans' from 'first Europeans'. Look much further back than the medieval period.
questions.prompt: The first people to reach the Americas were the Vikings, led by Leif Erikson, who landed in Newfoundland around 1000 CE.

feedback.correct: That's right — the Vikings (Leif Erikson at L'Anse aux Meadows, ~1000 CE, documented in archaeology and the Vinland Sagas) were the first known *Europeans*, not the first people. Indigenous peoples migrated from Asia via Beringia at least 15,000 years ago — possibly ~23,000 (White Sands footprints, New Mexico).
feedback.incorrect: Actually false. The Vikings (Leif Erikson, L'Anse aux Meadows, ~1000 CE) were the first known *Europeans* in the Americas, but Indigenous peoples had been there for at least 15,000 years — possibly ~23,000 — having crossed from Asia via Beringia.

questions.title: Lightning Strikes
questions.prompt: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.

feedback.correct: Correct — this is a folk saying, not a fact. Tall structures like the Empire State Building are struck dozens of times per year.
feedback.incorrect: Actually false. The saying is folklore. Tall objects (skyscrapers, mountain peaks, lightning rods) are routinely struck multiple times — the Empire State Building is hit 20-25 times a year on average.

questions.title: Speed of Sound in Water
questions.hint: Sound travels faster through denser media because the molecules are closer together and pass vibrations on more quickly.
questions.prompt: Sound travels faster in water than in air.

feedback.correct: Correct — sound moves at about 1,480 m/s in water versus 343 m/s in air. Whales use this for long-range communication.
feedback.incorrect: Actually true. Sound is roughly 4× faster in water (1,480 m/s) than in air (343 m/s) because water molecules are packed more tightly.

questions.title: Capital of Brazil
questions.hint: Rio is famous (Carnival, Christ the Redeemer), but the capital was deliberately moved inland in 1960.
questions.prompt: The capital of Brazil is Rio de Janeiro.

feedback.correct: Correct — Brazil's capital is Brasília, a planned city built inland that became capital in 1960. Rio was the capital before that.
feedback.incorrect: Actually false. Rio de Janeiro was Brazil's capital until 1960, when the seat of government moved to the newly-built Brasília.

feedback.correct: Correct — sharks are fish (cartilaginous fish, class Chondrichthyes). They breathe through gills and lay eggs or give live birth depending on species.
feedback.incorrect: Actually false. Sharks are fish, not mammals. They have gills, not lungs, and a skeleton made of cartilage rather than bone. Whales and dolphins are the marine mammals you might be thinking of.

questions.title: Largest Desert on Earth
questions.hint: A 'desert' is defined by precipitation, not by sand or temperature. Where on Earth gets the least rain or snowfall annually?
questions.prompt: Antarctica is the largest desert in the world.

feedback.correct: Correct — deserts are defined by low precipitation (under 250 mm/year), not by heat or sand. Antarctica receives almost no precipitation and covers ~14 million km², making it the largest desert on Earth. The Sahara is the largest hot desert.
feedback.incorrect: Actually true. The technical definition of a desert is precipitation under 250 mm/year, not heat or sand. Antarctica fits and covers ~14 million km² — larger than the Sahara, which is the largest hot desert.

questions.title: Chemical Symbol for Gold
questions.hint: Many element symbols come from Latin names. Gold's Latin name is 'aurum'.
questions.prompt: The chemical symbol for gold is Au.

feedback.correct: Correct — Au comes from the Latin 'aurum'. Other Latin-derived symbols you may know: Ag (silver, argentum), Fe (iron, ferrum), Pb (lead, plumbum).
feedback.incorrect: Actually true. The symbol Au derives from the Latin name for gold, 'aurum'. Other elements with Latin-based symbols include Ag (silver), Fe (iron), and Na (sodium, from natrium).
